planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil; space closely for a clipped hedge.

directions: This glossy-leaved hybrid, long sold in nurseries simply as wall germander, is actually a cross between Teucrium chamaedrys and the tenderer T. lucidum and is the plant most commonly used for clipped knot-garden edging and dwarf hedging in place of boxwood. Shear once or twice a season to maintain a tight, formal line, ideally right after the two-lipped rose-purple flowers fade in midsummer. Give it neutral to slightly alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun, since heavy or waterlogged ground quickly leads to root rot. It rarely sets viable seed, so propagate named stock from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late summer.

common_name: Azureum Bush Germander (Deep Blue-Flowered Silver Shrub Germander)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sharply drained soil; site in a sheltered, hot spot where winters flirt with zone 8.

directions: An RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of shrubby germander chosen for flowers of a richer violet-blue than the species, set off by felted, silvery-white new growth and stems. Use it as an informal silver hedge, windbreak, or clipped screen in coastal and Mediterranean-climate gardens, shearing after the main spring-to-summer flush to keep it dense. It is damaged below roughly 15 degrees F, so gardeners at the cold edge of its range should site it against a warm wall and mulch the root zone before winter. Thrives in poor, gritty, alkaline soil and resents rich, moisture-retentive ground.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; spaces well between paving stones or along wall tops.

directions: A mat-forming selection of wall germander that spreads by underground stolons into a dense, glossy, oak-leaf-textured carpet rarely more than a few inches tall, useful as a tough groundcover on slopes, in gravel gardens, and cascading over rock walls. Deep pink to purple flower whorls appear in loose spikes through early summer and draw bees readily. Unlike the type species it tolerates light foot traffic and a range of soils, though it still performs best with sharp drainage and resents constantly wet ground. Shear lightly after bloom to tidy the mat and keep it spreading densely rather than getting woody and sparse in the center.
sources: Mountain States Wholesale Nursery plant guide

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, gritty, well-drained soil; excellent for rock gardens, edging, and containers where full-size santolina is too large.

directions: The most diminutive of the cotton lavenders, forming a tight, rounded button of finely dissected silver-gray foliage that rarely exceeds a foot tall, well suited to rock gardens, dry stone walls, and the front of a gravel border where larger santolinas would overwhelm. Small, bright yellow button flowers appear on short stalks in summer and can be left for texture or clipped off to keep the silver mound tidy. Shear lightly after flowering and again in early spring to prevent the center from opening up and going woody, a common problem with aging santolinas. Give it poor to average, sharply drained soil and avoid rich or damp ground, which shortens its life considerably.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; propagate by cuttings since variegation does not come true from seed.

directions: A woody-based, bushy wallflower whose narrow gray-green leaves are edged in cream, giving the mound a two-toned glow even before the lilac-to-lavender flower spikes open from spring through fall with sporadic winter flushes in mild climates. Grow in lean to average, slightly alkaline soil and keep on the dry side through summer, since damp or overly fertile conditions shorten its already brief lifespan. Deadhead spent racemes to prolong flowering and shear lightly after the main spring flush to keep growth compact and prevent woodiness. Plants tend to fade after two or three seasons, so root softwood cuttings periodically to keep young replacements coming along.
